text: Question four. How do you deduplicate to the latest record per key? Number each customer's rows from the newest with row number, and keep row one. The page's table holds twenty-four updates from twelve customers, and twelve rows come out. The filter goes in a wrapping query, because where can't see a window function. Postgres says so. Group by with max finds each customer's latest time, but loses the email that goes with it. The follow-up is a tie. Give customer three a second update at the very same second. Rank numbers both of them one, so thirteen rows come back. Row number keeps one, but which one is the engine's choice. Add a tiebreaker to the order by, like a load sequence number, so every run keeps the same row. Postgres's distinct on does the same in one line, but only Postgres has it. Question five. What does qualify do, and how does it relate to where and having? Where filters raw rows. Having filters groups. Qualify filters on a window function's result, so it runs last: where, then group by and having, then the windows, then qualify. So the wrapping query goes. Postgres has no qualify, so this runs in DuckDB, an analytics database, and keeps the same twelve rows. The cloud data platforms Snowflake, BigQuery and Databricks support it too. On Postgres, keep the subquery. Back to the frame, the part of over that decides what a total includes.
